title: Rav Huna (in Rav Ashi’s Time)
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman laments that this Rav Huna has been forgotten like a dead man from the heart. Wherever the compilers found Rav Huna with Rav Ashi, they agreed and concluded that it is an earlier Rav Ashi, whom Hyman rejects as nonexistent, as he explains in the entry Rav Ashi. Hyman argues from the Gemara that he discusses matters only with Rav Ashi, the arranger of the Talmud, as in Shabbat 42a: “Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua said: I saw Rava … Rav Huna said to Rav Ashi: Perhaps it is different there”; here there is no room to speak of an earlier Rav Ashi, for it refers to the words of Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua. Likewise we find in Shabbat 60b, “Rav Huna asked Rav Ashi,” and in Avodah Zarah 60b he raised an objection to Rav Ashi. Hyman concludes from this that he sat before Rav Ashi. But what we find in Shabbat 37b, “Rav Ashi said: I was standing before Rav Huna,” and Bava Kamma 114a, “Rav Ashi said: When we were at Rav Huna’s,” Hyman instead proposes “at Rav Kahana’s,” according to Dikdukei Soferim’s reading, and so is the Rosh’s reading.

Hyman reports that the Gaon, author of Dorot HaRishonim, in part 3, explained with clear proofs that this Rav Huna was the husband of the sister of Ravina, Rav Ashi’s colleague; he died young and left after him two sons who afterward were among the great men of the generation: (1) Rav Nachman bar Rav Huna, who headed the academy in Sura after Rav Idi bar Avin and died thirty years after Rav Ashi, in year 667 (תרסז in the supplied transcription; era unspecified here), which Hyman attributes to the Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon, part 3, chapter 3; and the second is the later Ravina, as cited there: “On the thirteenth of Kislev in year 811 (תתיא; Hyman proposes 786, תשפו) died Rabbana Avina son of Rav Huna, who is Ravina, and he is the end of instruction.” This is what they said in Ketubot 100b: “Ravina had in his possession the wine of Ravina Zuta, an orphan, his sister’s son … he came before Rav Ashi.” Hyman finds this name nowhere else; only here, when he is mentioned together with his uncle Ravina, and he was then a young orphan, therefore they mentioned him by this name; but afterward everyone knew the difference between him and his uncle, and therefore they called him Ravina without further designation. His mother always transmitted to him his father’s conduct, as in Berakhot 39b: “Ravina said: My mother told me: Your father acted according to Rabbi Chiyya”; and likewise Menachot 68b: “Your father did not eat,” etc.

Likewise Mareimar transmitted to him his father’s teaching, as in Nedarim 60b: “Ravina said: Mareimar told me: Thus said your father in Rav Yosef’s name”; and there, 90a: “Mareimar told me: Thus said your father in Rav Pappi’s name.” Hyman considers it impossible that this is Ravina, Rav Ashi’s colleague, who was much older than Mareimar; how would Mareimar tell him things in his father’s name? He regards this as clear.

notes.text: p002 remains held: supplied תרסז=667 conflicts with thirty years after RavAshi under the surrounding chronology. Preserve667,811 and Hyman’s proposed786 rather than repair dates automatically; no era conversion. Saved Davidson Berakhot39b explicitly RabbiChiyya, supporting that expansion. Hyman/DorotHaRishonim’s orphan/uncle genealogy and RavHuna/Kahana proposals remain scoped arguments, not a merged identity.

The earlier note predates the comparison of the printed sources. The supplied transcription gives תרסז (667), while Hyman’s London edition (vol. I, p. 346) prints תרסו (666). The Oxford 1888 edition of the Epistle of Rav Sherira Gaon (pp. 33–34; digital 1:108) gives תשסו (766) for Rav Nachman’s death and תשלח (738) for Rav Ashi’s. The difference there is 28 years, alongside Hyman’s “thirty years.” The same Epistle passage records Avina son of Rav Huna’s death on 13 Kislev in the year 811. The proposed 786 is Hyman’s emendation. The year numbers are given without converting calendars.

The question about nails in a sandal appears in Shabbat 60b in the consulted edition. Hyman cites 60a. Shabbat 42a first names Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, then gives the name Rav Huna without a patronymic in the exchange with Rav Ashi. The consulted Shabbat 37b and Bava Kamma 114a name Rav Huna. The Rosh (Bava Kamma 10:14) names Rav Kahana in the corresponding passage about testimony. Hyman’s statement about Dikdukei Soferim and his wider reconstruction are retained as his own.

Ketubot 100b explicitly calls Ravina the younger an orphan and the older Ravina’s sister’s son. The older Ravina takes the question about the boy’s wine to Rav Ashi. The case leaves the boy’s father unnamed. The identification and the account of the two sons are the reconstruction Hyman attributes to Dorot HaRishonim.

Berakhot 39b and Menachot 68b report what Ravina’s mother told him about his father’s practices. The first names Rabbi Chiyya and the second concerns eating the new grain on the night leading into 18 Nisan. In Nedarim 60b the consulted Hebrew puts Yosef in brackets in the transmission from Mareimar. Nedarim 90a names Rav Pappi. Hyman draws his own conclusion about which Ravina heard these traditions.
